Issued at 1200 PM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

A vigorous shortwave continues moving southeast from IA this morning 
through Central IL today, reaching central IN this afternoon. The 
eventual placement of the warm front will be key in understanding 
severity, but there appears to be some southward trend in that 
placement in models between yesterday and today. Key to thunderstorm 
development appears to be the mid level lapse rates. Hail was 
forming across eastern IA this morning right on the northern 
gradient from high to low within an elevated area of instability. 
This would be the cause of hail should it form across the area 
today. Such an area of mid level lapse rates moves into areas south 
of US-30 midday into the afternoon before vacating by 20z. This area 
is well out in front of the forcing and would likely not be where 
storms form. The other area into our southwest 1 to 2 tiers of 
counties has mid level lapse rates from 6.5 to 7C. This overlaps 
with an area of very weak MUCAPE right around 100 to 250 J/kg in the 
20 to 00z window. There is some low level turning to work with 
within the lowest 1 to 2km of the atmosphere, but given the weak 
instability and what appears to be an elevated instability nature to 
the atmospheric column, the tornado threat appears to be low unless 
we can realize a taller surface instability column. Soundings appear 
to show a sort of an onion-shaped or shallow inverted-V profile that 
may be conducive to bringing winds down to the surface alluding to 
the gusty to damaging wind possibility. 

Hot on the heels of this wave is an area of vorticity traveling 
southward from Canada. As this area travels southward, it
deepens and interacts with the departing low pressure area. 
What's interesting is the deeper cold is delayed and farther 
west of Lk MI on Thursday. The ECMWF almost has a drainage 
signal where the eastern Lk MI area is cold, but over the lake 
is warmer, even at 850 mb. So, while the QPF signal appears lake
effect/lake enhanced, we haven't gotten the cold air enough to 
change it over to snow yet. A couple of compact waves traverse 
southward nearby Lk MI and the RRFS seems to show a trough 
kicking off a more sustained band Thursday evening. By the time 
we get to early Fri AM, enough cold air has wrapped in that 
soundings are beginning to get snow mixed in or changed over. -5
to -6C at 850 mb is right over the southern tear drop of Lk MI 
on the ECMWF so that makes sense. As various waves/instability 
troughs traverse southward, finding the exact trajectory will be
difficult because there will be some east-west wavering. A 
slight eastward change can mean the relatively vigorous lift 
going on from the relatively warm lake and cold airmass 
interaction can mean quick snow rates getting into LaPorte and 
maybe Starke counties. These could be rates that overcome the 
warm ground from how anomalously warm we've been this late fall.
As such, will continue the mention of the 1 to 2 inches of snow
through Friday that could result in LaPorte county especially 
with that wavering. Model guidance with variable snow ratios 
continues to back this up. It'll be interesting to see what 
happens with snow and if it'll stay mainly on grassy surfaces or
if it'll have enough oomph to accumulate on roads. Some 
guidance say it'll struggle to accumulate on roads Friday 
morning. The snow band may push eastward Saturday morning toward
US-30, but it would appear to be more diffuse at that point and
in its dying trend. It'll also trend back to rain or drizzle as
the column warms. Lake clouds could continue through Sunday 
with the northwest trajectories continuing. It is interesting to
see the highs are still forecast to warm into the 40s on Friday
and Saturday. That would cut into the accumulation ceilings and
I'm curious if we'd have refreezing overnight with sub-freezing
lows. This would depend on having standing water left on roads 
that, with light to calm wind, would indicate it's possible. 

Finally, by the time we get to Monday, trajectories change even as 
the last vigorous wave traverses the lake Saturday. Surface high 
pressure is already working to dry low level moisture out this 
weekend. Highs trend warmer through the 40s to reach the 50s by the 
middle of next week as the surface high slowly translates eastward. 
There is a vigorous wave south of the high that moves into the Gulf 
States, but it's far enough south to avoid our area. The warm 
advection pattern returns midweek next week as a wave shifts 
northeastward from the Central Plains into south-central Canada. As 
a result, the work week looks dry Monday through at least Thursday. 
However, lows won't rise above freezing until Thursday morning.
